questions.q: What approaches have researchers used to reduce hallucinations in language models?
questions.summary: Researchers have employed various methods to reduce hallucinations in language models, including Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) [P1], which decreases hallucinations on list-based questions, and DoLa [P8], which improved truthfulness on TruthfulQA by 12 to 17 absolute percentage points. These findings suggest that active validation and contrasting layers can effectively mitigate hallucinations.

DoLa improved LLaMA models' truthfulness on TruthfulQA by 12 to 17 absolute percentage points without retrieved knowledge or additional fine-tuning.

questions.q: How do you measure factual precision in long-form generation?
questions.summary: Factual precision in long-form generation is measured by breaking down the text into atomic facts and evaluating the percentage of these facts supported by reliable knowledge sources, as seen in the FActScore method [P1]. This approach provides a finer-grained measure compared to simply judging the entire output as true or false.

passages.label: P3
passages.text: Models can also be trained to predict P(IK), the probability that they know the answer to a question; this partly generalizes across tasks, though calibration on new tasks is weaker.

passages.label: P4
passages.text: Larger models were generally less truthful because they imitate popular falsehoods more effectively; the authors argue that scaling alone is less promising for truthfulness than fine-tuning with objectives other than imitating web text.

passages.label: P5
passages.text: The authors conclude that models mostly acquire factual knowledge during pretraining while fine-tuning teaches them to use it, and that early stopping reduces the hallucination risk from new-knowledge examples.

passages.label: P6
passages.text: The paper shows a statistical lower bound on the rate at which calibrated pretrained language models hallucinate arbitrary facts whose truth cannot be determined from the training data.

passages.label: P7
passages.text: The best retrieval-augmented models reach state-of-the-art results on knowledge-grounded conversation tasks and generalize better to topics unseen in training.

passages.label: P8
passages.text: An automated estimator that uses retrieval and a strong language model approximates human FActScore with an error rate below 2%, which makes large-scale factuality evaluation practical.

passages.label: P9
passages.text: Intervention strength controls a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness, and the truthful directions can be located with only a few hundred labeled examples, which makes the method data-efficient.

passages.label: P10
passages.text: Self-RAG trains a single language model to retrieve passages on demand and to generate reflection tokens that judge whether retrieval is needed, whether passages are relevant, and whether its own output is supported by them.

passages.label: P11
passages.text: Across several generation tasks, RARR significantly improved attribution while preserving the original input to a greater degree than earlier editing models.

passages.label: P12
passages.text: CoVe decreased hallucinations on list-based questions from Wikidata, closed-book MultiSpanQA and long-form biography generation.

questions.q: How can knowledge in a language model be updated without retraining?
questions.summary: Knowledge in a language model can be updated without retraining by using retrieval-augmented generation [P2] or by using reflection tokens [P8]. These methods allow for the incorporation of new knowledge or the control of model responses without the need for full retraining.

findings_detail.finding: Knowledge can be updated by replacing documents in a document index without retraining the model, allowing for the correction of outdated facts.
Reflection tokens enable users to control the model's responses, trading citation precision for completeness without retraining.
